chapter: Reel 2: Los Angeles musicians, the Apex and Cotton Club
title: The 1935 opening of the new Apex at 55th and Central
summary: Mrs. Howard reads a California News account and ad: Curtis Moseby hosting, Sue Hoye, Patsy Hunter's revue and Buck Clayton's band.

bands.name: Buck Clayton and his Harlem Gentlemen Orchestra

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: Mrs. Howard found a copy of the California News, which was for the day of Saturday, November 9, 1935, and this was a newspaper published in the 3700 block of South Central Avenue. And there's a story here on the Apex, where she had just opened. Okay?

I believe so, I believe so. The long-awaited return of Curtis Moseby to the local amusement world came to an end last week. That's Wednesday night. When the doors of the new Apex Club at 55th and Central Avenue were swung open to a brilliant gathering of celebrities there to witness the occasion.
Large and beautiful auditorium that houses the club was quietly filled to capacity. Numerous celebrities of the

stage and screen who remembered Mr. Moseby for his past reputation of providing only the best of entertainers, and lavish amounts were notified in the throngs. Occupying the role of MC, Moseby has his old self again, the perfect host. Everyone felt themselves at home when Bill Robinson, from his ringside table, began calling up on some of the celebrities present who evidently were bent on keeping themselves unnoticed to stand up and take a bow.

" Mr. and Mrs. Bill Robinson had as their table guest Mr. David Butler, director of the 20th Century Fox film, The Littlest Rebel, in which Bill is featured. Among the other noticeables observed, Waller -- "
I think you dropped a line there.
Yeah. " Martha and Cliff Ritchie, Harvey Brooks, Pinkie Tomlin, Baby Mack, Dan Toby, Fred Solomon, Eddie Anderson, Clifton Bennett, and scores of others, including movie stars and directors.

" Mr. Curtis Moseby and Herman Hill came in for applause. After presenting one of the most pretentious floor reviews currently in the West. Patsy Hunter, the producer, was paid a remarkable tribute for her well-received efforts. The floor review was wisely presented, in that it does not attempt to place any individual star, but rather presents a well-balanced bill that spells a good show.
" One of the principals were warmly received as they
as they came on. Sue Hoye, a real favorite, proved that she will retain -- retains her hold on the crowds. Her singing numbers were pleasing.

"Consuela Harris, a newcomer, was pleasing in her dance numbers. She is a real beauty, And Gertrude Saunders is found a clever singing and dancing comedienne. One will have travel a long way to find a comedian who can top that fellow, Billy Mitchell. Miss Hunter has assembled a line of beautiful and smooth dancing chorines, eight in all, that (unintelligible) -- that's it, should be execute her routine in perfect time and rhythm. They're beautifully costumed in keeping with the tone of the place.
"Buck Clayton and his Harlem Gentlemen Orchestra supply the tantalizing music for the patrons as well as the floor reviews. Food and drinks are the highest quality."

Ad for the opening. Curtis Moseby's Club Apex, Central Avenue at 55th Street presents Gertrude Saunders, star of Shuffle Along, Blackbirds, Connie Harris, direct from Connie's Inn in New York and Black Bolero, the Three Chocklateers, those fast steppers in hot steps, Sue Hoye, former Club Apex star, Billy Mitchell, New York's funniest comedian. A laugh riot. Patsy Hunter and her tap-dance deluxe, Rudolph Duvall, the dancing fool, Ruth Gibbons, the girl with
the golden voice. All of these stars and a bevy of beautiful chorines to three different floor shows nightly, with Buck Clayton and his Harlem Gentlemen.
Meet the celebrities at the Apex. For reservations, phone Adam 9-473. Cover charge.
